name: IPS⁴o (In-place Parallel Super Scalar Samplesort)
workload: Sorting 2^10 to 2^32 uniformly-distributed 64-bit floating point elements (also Pair/Quartet/100Bytes records and skewed distributions), sequential and multi-core, on four different server machines.
claimed_speedup: Sequential IS4o is at least a factor of 1.86 faster than GCC's std::sort (and dual-pivot quicksort) for n=2^32 Uniform input on the Intel4S machine (1.57x on AMD1S); parallel IPS4o outperforms its closest non-in-place competitors by 2.26x on average (up to 2.78x for in-place competitors) on Intel2S for n>=2^26.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.2.0, -march=native -O3; OpenMP used for the parallel algorithm
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1800X 8-core, 32GiB RAM (AMD1S); 2x Intel Xeon E5-2683 v4 16-core, 512GiB RAM (Intel2S); 4x Intel Xeon E5-4640 8-core, 512GiB RAM (Intel4S)
stars_or_usage: 135 stars (canonical repo); used as the reference sequential/parallel sorting baseline in numerous follow-up algorithm-engineering papers and benchmark suites (e.g. PPQSort)
tradeoffs: Needs C++14; parallel mode requires OpenMP or std::thread plus TBB and 16-byte atomic compare-and-exchange support (or -mcx16/libatomic); does not compile on Windows; least advantage on already-sorted or low-cardinality inputs where n<=2^15.
caveats: Numbers are from the peer-reviewed ESA 2017 paper (Figures 6-7), reproduced via the linked in-repo benchmark suite; the originally-cited repo (SaschaWitt/ips4o) is now marked deprecated in favor of the canonical ips4o/ips4o used here; parallel speedup shrinks to ~1.41x on the 4-socket NUMA machine (Intel4S) due to slower memory and interconnect.

name: BlockQuicksort
workload: Sorting arrays of random 32-bit ints, 10-dimensional double Vectors (Euclidean-norm comparator), and 21-field int Records, measured as elements sorted per second, against GCC's std::sort.
claimed_speedup: More than an 80% increase in elements sorted per second over GCC's std::sort on random integer data; smaller but still positive speedups on Vector/Record data; std::sort wins only on sorted or almost-sorted inputs.
hardware: Intel Core i5-2500K @ 3.30GHz, 4 cores, 32KB L1 i/d, 256KB L2/core, 6MB shared L3, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04.4 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; algorithm published in ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics (2019) and cited as the 'closest sequential competitor' baseline in the IPS4o paper
tradeoffs: In-place but not stable; block size (default 128) needs tuning per data type; branch-misprediction-avoidance technique now widely reused (e.g. pdqsort, PPQSort) under more permissive licenses than this repo's GPL-3.0.
caveats: Repo unmaintained since Nov 2021; the std::sort compared against is a bundled copy of GCC 4.7.2's libstdc++ implementation (see paper footnote 3), not necessarily the std::sort of the g++ 4.8.4 compiler used to build the test; no libc++ or MSVC STL comparison.

name: Boost.Sort — spreadsort
workload: Sorting 100,000,000 random 64-bit integers, 10,000,000 random strings, and up to 100,000,000 random small objects (8-512 bytes) compared by a heavy or light comparator, single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: spreadsort ~1.94x faster than std::sort sorting 100M random 64-bit ints (8.2154s vs 4.2248s); ~2.57x faster sorting 10M random strings (6.2442s vs 2.4323s); ~1.6x faster on 100M 8-byte objects with a heavy comparator (8.25s vs 5.10s).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3 on Linux (exact optimization flags beyond the standard Boost.Build release configuration are not stated in the doc)
hardware: Intel Core i7-5820K @ 3.30GHz, 6 cores / 2 threads per core, 15MB cache
stars_or_usage: 58 stars on the standalone mirror repo; ships as part of Boost, one of the most widely deployed C++ library collections
tradeoffs: spreadsort is unstable and needs O(key_length) extra memory; it is a hybrid radix/comparison sort so wins depend on key bit-width/distribution; the library's other stable algorithms (spinsort, flat_stable_sort) were NOT faster than std::stable_sort on uniformly random data in this same benchmark, only on near-sorted inputs.
caveats: Benchmark authored by the library's own maintainers, not an independent third party; exact compiler optimization flags are not spelled out; hardware (i7-5820K, GCC 6.3) dates to around the library's 2017 Boost release, not re-run on recent hardware/toolchains.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/boostorg/sort/contents/doc/linux_single.qbk (repo located via gh search repos "radix sort faster")

name: quadsort
workload: Sorting 100,000 random 32-bit/64-bit/128-bit-payload elements and small arrays (4-4096 items) across many distributions (random, ascending, descending, sawtooth, pipe-organ, bit-reversal), best-of-100 runs.
claimed_speedup: ~2.4x faster than std::stable_sort at 1024 random 32-bit items (0.013871s vs 0.005664s, best-of-100); several-x faster on partially-ordered distributions (e.g. ~16x on ascending-saw, ~10x on pipe-organ).
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive (GCC 7.5.0, WSL2/Ubuntu 18.04); a separate run used clang -O3 (clang 10)
tradeoffs: Stable, needs O(n) swap buffer like std::stable_sort; branchless design is tuned for GCC on x86 — author notes a 2-3x slowdown for the branchless merge/small-sort routines when compiled with clang instead of gcc.
caveats: First-party benchmark (author's own 'wolfsort' suite), not independently replicated; CPU/hardware model is never stated in the README (only the WSL2/Ubuntu version), so the exact numbers are not independently reproducible; GCC 7.5.0 toolchain is dated.

name: fluxsort
workload: Sorting 100,000 random 32-bit elements across many distributions (random, ascending, descending, sawtooth, pipe-organ, bit-reversal), best-of-100 runs.
claimed_speedup: ~3.2x faster than std::stable_sort on random-order 100K 32-bit ints (0.006113s vs 0.001906s, best-of-100); up to ~18x faster on ascending-order input (0.000804s vs 0.000044s).
tradeoffs: Stable quicksort/mergesort hybrid, needs O(n) auxiliary memory; same GCC/x86-tuning caveats as its sibling quadsort.
caveats: First-party benchmark suite (same author/suite as quadsort), hardware/CPU not stated, dated GCC 7.5.0 toolchain (2019-era WSL image).

name: x86-simd-sort
workload: Sorting arrays of custom 3D Point structs (float/double coordinates) via object_qsort, keyed by a coordinate value or by Manhattan/Euclidean/Chebyshev distance, on an AVX-512-capable x86 processor.
claimed_speedup: object_qsort up to 5x faster than std::sort for 32-bit-keyed objects and ~4x for 64-bit-keyed objects on simple single-field sorts; up to 10x faster when sorting by (more expensive) Euclidean distance.
hardware: unspecified CPU with AVX-512 support (README states only 'a processor with AVX-512')
stars_or_usage: 1027 stars; used as a submodule in NumPy (np.sort/argsort/partition/argpartition), PyTorch (torch.sort/argsort), and merged (modified) into OpenJDK
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 (or AVX2 fallback with fewer supported dtypes) x86 hardware; object_qsort needs O(N) extra memory for a key+index array; the library also ships qselect (std::nth_element-equivalent) and partial_qsort (std::partial_sort-equivalent) with similar SIMD speedups that were not separately benchmarked here.
caveats: The cited performance chart only says it was 'collected on a processor with AVX-512' — no specific CPU model, compiler, or flags are given for that figure, so the exact numbers are not independently reproducible as documented, even though the underlying Google Benchmark harness (benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp) is present and runnable in-repo.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "quicksort SIMD" / gh search repos "x86-simd-sort"

name: poor-circle/radix_sort
workload: Sorting 1 billion random int32 values, single-threaded and with std::execution::par.
claimed_speedup: radix_sort 14.28x faster than std::sort (91407ms vs 6402ms) and ~12.9x faster than std::stable_sort (82896ms vs 6402ms) for 1 billion int32; parallel radix_sort ~35.1x faster than std::sort (91407ms vs 2603ms).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC, Release configuration (exact compiler version and flags not stated)
tradeoffs: LSD radix sort restricted to keys with a defined 'radix trait' (integers, floats, pointers, pairs, user structs via traits) rather than arbitrary-comparator sorting like std::sort; needs an O(n) auxiliary buffer (user-suppliable).
caveats: Single-author project, unmaintained since Jan 2022; MSVC version/flags not specified so not fully reproducible; no GCC/Clang or libstdc++/libc++ comparison is given, only MSVC STL.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sort faster than std::sort"

name: vxsort-cpp
workload: Sorting int64/int32 arrays of 4,096 to 1,048,576 elements on a single core, comparing SIMD vxsort (AVX2/AVX-512, several unroll factors) against a scalar introsort baseline.
claimed_speedup: ~4.8x faster than the scalar 'Introspective Sort' baseline for 1M int64 elements with 8x unroll (55ns/elem vs 11.5ns/elem); ~4.5x faster at 128K elements.
compiler_and_flags: Clang recommended in the README ('for better code-gen'); exact optimization level / CMake build type used for the published numbers is not stated
tradeoffs: Requires AVX2/AVX-512 x86 hardware; C++ port of the original C# VxSort library, described by its own author as an experimental/rough reimplementation; low adoption relative to other SIMD sorts in this list.
caveats: The README labels its baseline 'Introspective Sort (Scalar Baseline)', not literally std::sort; the repo separately contains a bench/fullsort/BM_fullsort.stdsort.cpp target that calls std::sort() directly, but it could not be confirmed that the published README numbers came from that exact target rather than a hand-written scalar reference; the documented build steps (cmake && make) do not pin a Release build type, so the published numbers may not reflect a fully optimized build. Baseline and methodology treated as best-guess; confidence lowered accordingly.
